title: Tansy and the Midnight Mission
markdown:
The amulet pulsed. A shy gold beat, no louder than a held breath, ticked through the Egyptian gallery and into the marble.

Tansy’s whiskers twitched. She was no ordinary tabby. She was a mummy cat, fur the colour of sun-baked dunes, eyes like chips of emerald, ancient as desert sand. She had spent the noisy morning on a rope stanchion while Hugo, the museum’s brilliant guide, stretched like a tiger and promised a spectacular day. The doors had clattered shut on the city’s boom. Now the moon kept watch, and the floor thrummed.

Hugo padded in, spectacles popping on his nose. “Goodness,” he whispered. “How did this curious trinket get here?”

A tall stone warrior jiggled. An inch. No more.

“Did you perceive that, Tansy?”

Tansy flicked her tail. She had felt it: a fizzy prickle, the sort that makes pots remember they were once useful and statues remember they had errands.

A sky-blue porcelain vase had inched toward the edge of its plinth.

“If the treasures keep dancing, they’ll shatter,” Hugo said. “And dawn is just around the bend.”

Tansy nudged his hand. We shall manage this, said the nudge.

“Right you are,” Hugo declared, booming even at a whisper. “A midnight mission. Every artifact back where it belongs before the sun tickles the city awake.”

Thus the Great Museum Midnight Dash began.

Crisis one: the Roman wing. A miniature chariot had nudged a golden laurel wreath onto the floor. Hugo picked it up as if it might bruise.

“Easy does it, my fine friend.” He set the wreath back like a king’s crown. Tansy sat, tail neat, until the chariot remembered it was a model and not a getaway.

They had a breath in the hush. Dust hung. Hugo’s spectacles fogged, then cleared. Forward, then.

Crisis two was worse. Past the colossal T-Rex, a fossilized tooth had slid from its stand. Tansy leapt to a tall case. One delicate tap. The tooth rolled, settled, clicked home as if it had only been stretching. Brilliant, Hugo’s face said, but there was no time for speeches. Through the Hall of Precious Gems a sapphire ring had slipped its cushion. Hugo nudged it back.

“We wouldn’t want jewel-related confusion.”

Hours thinned. Each exhibit was a puzzle. Hugo knew where things belonged. Tansy reached the impossible spots, a swift shadow of dune-coloured fur, paws silent on marble that still held the day’s warmth. They passed a knight whose visor had tried a wink and thought better of it. Hugo chuckled once, dry as old paper, and they did not linger. The sky outside went from black to a rumour of grey.

Then the Grand Gallery. The T-Rex’s massive foot had shifted forward an inch and was kissing a velvet rope. That was the worst of it: bone the size of a door, dawn in the glass, and no more inches to spare.

“Oh, blazes and botheration,” Hugo whispered. “The grand finale.”

He pushed. The bone did not care. Tansy chirped, squeezed through the smallest gap in the rib cage, and shoved from inside with all her minuscule, ancient cat might.

Hugo found a second wind. Together they heaved. The colossal foot eased back, inch by stubborn inch, as the first sliver of sun peeked over the rooftops.

They stood breathless. Gold light streamed in. Dust motes turned lazy circles. Everything — pots, wreath, tooth, ring, foot — was where it ought to be. The museum was safe, and, more to the point, still itself.

Tansy stretched. Hugo knelt. “We did it, Tansy. What a night.”

The halls filled with the promise of a new day. Hugo’s voice, which had spent hours being careful, found its morning again.

“Today,” he said, and Tansy’s ears flicked toward the doors that would soon burst open, “is going to be amazing!”
characters: Hugo (the museum guide), Tansy (a mummy cat)
